category: Self-hosted password and secrets management for organisations: a team password manager for people (personal vault, sharing, browser autofill, emergency access) combined with a write-without-read secret store, leases and a private certificate authority for applications, running inside the organisation's own Nextcloud with zero-knowledge encryption. A buyer, typically a Dutch public body wanting credentials kept on its own infrastructure, compares it with the SaaS team password managers (Bitwarden, 1Password, Keeper), the self-hosted open-source team manager Passbolt, the machine-secrets engine HashiCorp Vault for the application side, and the community Nextcloud Passwords app as the in-platform alternative. Decided from the code on 2026-09-26 (appinfo/info.xml, lib/Controller, 45 specs under openspec/specs); no prior competitor research exists for this product under any of its names.

capabilities.name: Share a secret with a Nextcloud group.

built.evidence: lib/Controller/GroupShareController.php and lib/Service/GroupShareService.php implement group shares fully, but src/components/share/GroupShareForm.vue (registry key 'group-share-form') has no cnOpenModal caller anywhere in src/, and no store or component ever calls the /api/v1/secrets/{id}/group-shares endpoints (grep -rn 'group-shares' src/ browser-extension/ cli/: no hits). GroupShareForm.vue also calls useShareStore.encryptForRecipient with a `members` prop no caller ever supplies, not the groupShare backend at all.
built.note: A user cannot share a secret with a Nextcloud group today. The backend and a form component exist but nothing in the app opens the form or calls the group-share API.

defects.what: Group-share form component is registered but never opened by any page or dialog, and its own submit logic calls the wrong store (useShareStore per-user encryption) rather than the group-shares endpoint.

capabilities.name: People who join a group later get access once the owner approves.

The owner picks this up by reopening src/modals/TeamFolderDialog.vue, whose refresh() (line 449) reconciles and shows a 'N members need re-share' banner (lines 148-181) with a button wired to onRunFanOut -> store.runFanOut -> POST /apps/keepiq/api/v1/team-folders/{id}/shares.
built.reachedOn: TeamFolderDialog (opened from SecretList.vue folder actions) -> reconcile banner -> Share now button
built.note: For team folders this works, but it is a blanket re-share of every pending member, not a per-request approve/deny: the dedicated store action teamFolder.js:202 approveJoin is never called from any component, so the individual-approval gesture the spec and the notification text describe does not exist in the UI. The separate ad-hoc group-share path (GroupShareController) that this row's specHint (user-sharing/spec.md) actually names has no UI at all (see sharing-02), so a GroupShare row is never created and its own owner-notification requirement never fires in practice.

defects.what: approveJoin is defined and calls a real backend route but no component ever calls it; the only reachable grant path is the blanket reconcile/Share-now fan-out.

capabilities.name: Ask the owner of a secret for access to it.

built.evidence: No feature lets a user who lacks any access to a secret ask its owner for access. The nearest built feature, src/components/share/ShareRequestForm.vue (mounted in SecretDetailSidebar.vue:687 for isRecipient && !isOwner), requires the requester to ALREADY hold a shared copy and asks the owner to share with a DIFFERENT third party (openspec/specs/user-sharing/spec.md#requirement-share-request-recipient-initiated), which is a distinct capability from the one this row describes.
built.note: Rename suggestion: the built and reachable ShareRequestForm feature is 'ask the owner to share this secret with someone else', not 'ask the owner for access to it' for yourself. There is no discovery mechanism for a secret you cannot already see, so a self-access request has nothing to attach to.

capabilities._rename: The reachable ShareRequestForm feature should be named 'ask the owner to share this secret with a third party', which is a different capability than this row describes.

capabilities.name: Renew or revoke a machine lease.

built.evidence: Revoke: src/components/application/ApplicationLeasesPanel.vue:141 onRevoke() -> useLeaseStore().revoke() -> DELETE /apps/keepiq/api/v1/leases/{id} -> appinfo/routes.php:325 leaseAdmin#revoke. Renew: lib/Controller/MachineLeaseController.php:renew() and appinfo/routes.php:320 POST /api/v1/app/leases/{id}/renew exist and are fully implemented, but nothing in src/, browser-extension/ or cli/ calls it, and the internal fetch path (MachineSecretResponseService::grantLease) reuses an existing lease rather than calling this endpoint
built.reachedOn: Admin/registrant revoke: Application detail page -> Machine leases panel. Renew: machine route with no known caller in this repo (routes-unmatched.txt: NO-REF)
built.note: Revoking a lease from the application detail page works end to end. The dedicated self-renew endpoint for a bearer-holding application has a full controller and service but no caller anywhere in this checkout, including the keepiq CLI itself; leases are extended by re-fetch/reuse instead.

defects.what: POST /api/v1/app/leases/{id}/renew has no known consumer in the frontend, extension or CLI; lease extension in practice happens via grantOrReuse on fetch, not via this endpoint.

capabilities.name: An administrator sets the lease time limit.

built.evidence: src/components/settings/MachineLeaseSection.vue:93-128 GET/PUT /apps/keepiq/api/settings/admin (lease_default_ttl_seconds, lease_max_ttl_seconds, lease_renewable, lease_revocation_blocks_refetch), wired into src/views/settings/Settings.vue:23
built.reachedOn: Settings page -> Machine leases section
built.note: The instance-wide default and maximum lease TTL, renewability and block-on-revoke are all admin-settable from Settings.

defects.what: The per-application lease-policy override endpoint (PUT /api/v1/applications/{id}/lease-policy) has no frontend caller; only the instance-wide default is reachable from the UI.

capabilities.name: Delete an application together with its secrets.

built.evidence: lib/Controller/ApplicationController.php:338 destroy() -> lib/Service/ApplicationService.php:201-221 delete(): removes the application row and cascades MachineLease + lease-policy rows only. The method's own docblock (line 216-218) reads: 'The full cascade (Secrets + EncryptionSuite + SecretRequests) lands with the dedicated build cycle once those services accept owner_type=application.' SecretService::deleteByApplication() exists but is only called from ApplicationSecretRequestService and SecretPlaceholderCleaner, never from ApplicationService::delete()
built.reachedOn: Application detail page -> admin delete action -> DELETE /apps/keepiq/api/v1/applications/{id}
built.note: The application-mgmt spec requires that deleting an application permanently deletes the application, its EncryptionSuite, and all its attributed secrets. The shipped delete only removes the application row and its lease rows; secrets and the EncryptionSuite are left behind, contradicting the spec's own scenario.

defects.what: Deleting an application does not cascade-delete its EncryptionSuite or its attributed secrets, despite the application-mgmt spec's Delete Application requirement mandating both; the code comment admits this is deferred.

capabilities.name: See which secrets belong to which application.

built.evidence: src/components/application/ApplicationSecretsPanel.vue:134 -> src/store/modules/application.js:317 listApplicationSecrets() -> GET /apps/keepiq/api/v1/secrets?ownerType=application&ownerId={id} -> SecretController#index; panel is mounted from src/views/ApplicationDetail.vue:123
built.reachedOn: Application detail page -> Secrets panel
built.note: An application's detail page lists the (ciphertext) secrets attributed to it by name, type and creation date.

capabilities.name: Fetch secrets in a CI pipeline from one command-line binary without writing plaintext to disk.

built.evidence: cli/ci.go:97-126 cmdCIRun() fetches+decrypts each named secret and injects it into the child process environment only (runChild in cli/main.go:281-289); no plaintext is written to disk (comment at ci.go:124)
built.reachedOn: keepiq CLI: `keepiq ci run <name> -- <cmd>`
built.note: The CLI is a single static Go binary that fetches, decrypts and injects secrets into a child process's environment for CI use, never touching disk.

capabilities.name: Read your own vault from the command line.

built.evidence: cli/main.go: cmdList/cmdShow/cmdGet (lines 160-222) authenticate with a Nextcloud app-password, fetch the active suite, unwrap the private key with the master password, and decrypt fields client-side via dcrypto.DecryptField
built.reachedOn: keepiq CLI: `keepiq list|show|get|copy` (human mode)
built.note: v1 of the CLI is deliberately read-only; every decryption happens in the CLI process itself so no key material reaches the server.

capabilities.name: Inject secrets into a Kubernetes cluster.

built.evidence: grep -rli 'kubernetes|k8s|helm' lib src cli browser-extension: no hits
built.note: No Kubernetes secret injection (operator, CSI driver, sidecar) exists; keepiq's machine surface is a plain HTTP+JWT API a cluster could call itself, but nothing ships to do that integration.

capabilities.name: Use a ready-made GitHub Actions or GitLab CI integration.

built.evidence: grep -rli 'github.action|gitlab.ci|.gitlab-ci' lib src cli browser-extension: no hits (only this repo's own CI workflows use GitHub Actions, which is unrelated to a keepiq integration product)
built.note: No ready-made GitHub Actions or GitLab CI step exists; a pipeline would have to install and script the keepiq CLI itself.

capabilities.name: Generate short-lived database credentials on demand.

built.evidence: grep -rli 'dynamic.*database|database.*credential|db.*secret.*engine' lib src: no hits; keepiq only stores and serves secrets a human or app already supplied, it does not generate short-lived database credentials itself
built.note: No dynamic secrets engine (database, cloud IAM, etc.) exists, unlike Vault/OpenBao.

capabilities.name: Rotate a database or service password automatically.

built.evidence: openspec/specs/rotation-expiry-policies/spec.md:9 describes 'expiry, an admin-default and user-override max-age policy, approaching/overdue reminders ... a proven mark-rotated flow' -- this is a reminder + manual mark-rotated flow (lib/Controller/RotationController.php, src/store/modules/rotation.js), not automatic rotation of the underlying credential at the target service
built.note: keepiq flags stale/expiring secrets and lets a user mark one rotated, but it never rotates a password at the destination service itself the way Vault/1Password-style rotation connectors do.

capabilities.name: Use client libraries for common programming languages.

built.evidence: cli/ is a single Go CLI (stdlib only) covering human read-only + CI fetch; no client SDKs for other languages exist (no python/node/java package in the repo)
built.reachedOn: keepiq CLI (Go binary, cross-compiled)
built.note: There is one cross-compiled CLI binary, not per-language client libraries; a Python or Node consumer would call the documented HTTP+JWT API directly with no official SDK.

capabilities.name: Manage secrets as code with a Terraform provider.

built.evidence: grep -rli 'terraform' . --include=*.md --include=*.php --include=*.go: no hits
built.note: No Terraform provider exists for managing keepiq secrets/applications as code.

capabilities.name: Other Conduction apps keep their connection credentials in the vault.

built.evidence: The machine secret-store API (discovery, RFC 7523 token exchange, by-name fetch, write-back) is fully built server-side and documented for exactly this use in docs/integration-openconnector.md and openspec/specs/secret-store-api/spec.md; the design docs name OpenConnector (now integriq) as the intended consumer
built.reachedOn: machine: documented for consumption by other Conduction apps (e.g. integriq) via /api/v1/app/*
built.note: This checkout only contains keepiq's own code; whether integriq or another Conduction app actually stores its connection credentials in keepiq today cannot be settled from here, only that keepiq ships and documents a ready contract for it.

capabilities.name: Encrypt and decrypt data for an application without storing it.

built.evidence: grep -n 'class.*Controller' lib/Controller | grep -i 'encrypt|transit|crypto': only EncryptionSuiteController (manages the user's own suite/keypair), no generic encrypt/decrypt-as-a-service endpoint that takes arbitrary application data
built.note: keepiq encrypts secret VALUES it stores; it has no Vault-Transit-style API where an application sends it arbitrary data to encrypt/decrypt without storing it.
